chapter: Race, unions and the color line
title: Black and white musicians and the unions
summary: Lala says the Black musicians had a separate arrangement, white bands rarely mixed, and he got permission from the union to play with outside men.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Was there a colored union back or another time when Buddy Bober was operating? No.
No. Riz Boykin was Riz Boykin. Riz Boykin was Riz Boykin. That's after you. Riz Boykin? Yeah, that was after you. Oh, I mean that was way after you. Johnny. That is a play for the old.
The colored men were on the white union. Bob Kay and those fellas. Well, you all used to play nine unions.

We had permission from the union to get out of that man. Oh, that Johnny Pijos. He's a livin'. He's living? Sure. How old is he? What did you mean him, Bill? Charlie Patsutzi from Bloxy? No? No. He must be these men. Oh, he can't be living. Yes, it is. I'm back to 1900 years old. I played over there with Sharky on the truck and he rode the old thing around us. Where did he get permission to see? To get outside men. You know anybody called that, Bloxy? Yes, I don't know. I hate Tutszi J.
Yeah. So they gave you permission, huh?
Was there a lot of mixed bands in those days? Did you frequently play with a colored guy in the band?

Well, the colored guys we played with, they never played with no colored players. They only played with white bands. Only one player with colored and white was P. Coop. Well, Stevens, Steven Burles. He used to play with Jake Stevens. You know? So, you know what I'd like to get right? Yellow Nunes. Was he colored? No. No. I wonder how that came about.
